title: New Scientist Story Ideas — Anxiety — October 2026

studies.title: Anxiety and depression fell among Ukrainian civilians even as the shelling got worse
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely surprising prospective result from an under-studied natural experiment, held back by a small, skewed online sample.
studies.the_study: Researchers tracked 208 Ukrainian civilian adults (80.8% female, mean age 29.4) at two time points — June 2023, during the optimism of the counteroffensive, and November 2023, after it stalled. Over those six months, objective threat indicators (artillery attacks, air raid alarms) rose and confidence in military success fell, yet average scores for generalized anxiety, depression and somatic symptoms all went *down*. The strongest predictor of who failed to improve was baseline sleep disturbance; being female predicted smaller reductions in depression, and older age predicted larger reductions in anxiety.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests psychological adaptation to chronic danger can proceed independently of whether the danger is actually receding — the mind appears to recalibrate to a new baseline rather than track objective risk. It also flags disrupted sleep as the thing that blocks that recalibration, which is a plausible, testable target for wartime mental health support.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on a Kyiv resident in November 2023 — more alarms, more artillery, less hope than in June — scoring lower on anxiety than they did five months earlier. The hook: habituation to catastrophe is real and measurable, and the people who don't habituate are the ones who aren't sleeping. Worth calling Anton Kurapov (Paris Lodron University of Salzburg / Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv), who is himself a Ukrainian researcher studying his own country's civilians. Frame carefully: falling symptom scores are not the same as being well.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on the science of "the new normal" — how fast humans adjust their fear baseline to pandemics, climate disasters, chronic street violence and war, and what the cost of that adjustment is. Pairs naturally with habituation research and allostatic load. Fits a long-read outlet such as *The Atlantic*, *Mosaic*-style science features, or a *Nature* news feature on war and mental health.
studies.caveats: Small N (208), self-reported outcomes only, online convenience sample that is 80% female and young (mean age 29), two waves only with no pre-war baseline, observational design (cannot establish causation), attrition and selection effects likely — people who deteriorated most may have dropped out, which could manufacture the apparent improvement. Population may not generalize to older or rural Ukrainians.

studies.title: Young men describe sex as a hazard to defuse rather than something to enjoy
studies.ns_score_reason: vivid, culturally live and genuinely unexpected, but qualitative with 31 interviews, so the evidence can only support a "here is a pattern worth testing" story.
studies.the_study: Researchers thematically analyzed 31 in-depth interviews with heterosexual men aged 18 to 32 — a cohort who came of age after consent became a central cultural conversation. The striking finding was how rarely the men described enjoying sex at all. Three themes dominated: anxiety and vigilance during encounters, moral worry about harming a partner, and shame that came as much from self-criticism as from anyone else's accusation. The authors characterize it as an inward turn, where the operative question shifts from "does she want this?" to "am I the kind of man who could get this wrong?"
studies.why_it_matters: It identifies a form of performance anxiety that is moral rather than physical, and that existing frameworks for male sexual dysfunction don't really capture. Not much changes clinically yet — this is hypothesis-generating — but it opens a line of enquiry into how rapidly shifting sexual norms register in individual psychology.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the quote: a young man comparing sex to defusing a bomb. The surprise is that a cultural shift intended to make sex safer has, for some men, produced a vigilance state that crowds out pleasure entirely — and that the harshest accuser in the room is usually the man himself. Open on one interviewee mentally auditing an encounter in real time. Call Jess Forrest at the Melbourne School of Public Health, and get a sex therapist to say whether they're seeing this in clinic. Avoid any framing that pits this against consent education; the men themselves aren't asking for less of it.
studies.wider_angle: A reported feature on the state of consent education — what it was designed to do, what it measurably achieves, and whether anyone has studied its emotional side-effects on the people receiving it. That's a story for an education or policy outlet (*Times Higher Education*, *The Guardian*'s long read, a public health magazine) rather than a brain-science desk.
studies.caveats: Small N (31) and qualitative by design — no prevalence claim is possible, and we cannot know whether these men are typical or a self-selecting minority willing to be interviewed about sex. No comparison group, no older cohort, no women's accounts of the same encounters. Single interview point; participants' own causal attribution to "the cultural climate" is their interpretation, not a measured effect.

studies.title: Reminding people of death makes them want children — and the effect is strongest in the chronically ill
studies.ns_score_reason: a provocative link between death anxiety and the fertility slump, but it rests on mortality-salience priming, a paradigm with a poor replication record.
studies.the_study: Across three experiments with Chinese adults — including a sample of people with chronic illnesses — researchers primed participants to think about their own death and measured responses to parent-child images, attitudes to fertility policy, stated fertility intentions, and how readily death-related thoughts came to mind. Mortality salience increased fertility intentions and produced more favorable evaluations of fertility policy; priming participants with thoughts of children reduced the spike in death-related thoughts. Among chronically ill participants, both the death-thought accessibility and the fertility-intention effects were amplified. The authors are explicit that they did not directly test the full mediational chain.
studies.why_it_matters: It proposes that wanting children functions partly as a psychological defense against death anxiety, which would make fertility decisions less economically rational than policymakers assume. Treat as a line of enquiry rather than an explanation for falling birth rates.
studies.pitch_angle: The counterintuitive hook — pronatalist governments pour money into childcare subsidies and tax breaks, while this work suggests the lever may be existential rather than financial. Open on the chronically ill participants, in whom the effect was strongest. Call the Shandong Normal University group (Cuixia Zhao). But the honest spine of the piece is the tension: terror management theory is one of social psychology's most heavily cited frameworks and one of its least reliably replicated, so build in a replication-skeptic voice and keep the claim at "intentions in a lab," not "babies."
studies.wider_angle: A critical feature on the replication status of terror management theory three decades on — what has survived multi-lab scrutiny, what hasn't, and why the framework remains so attractive to researchers and commentators. That's a story for a psychology-focused or metascience outlet, or a *Science* news feature.
studies.caveats: Sample sizes not reported in the abstract; mortality-salience priming paradigms have repeatedly failed large multi-lab replication attempts; outcome is stated intention, not behavior; single-country (Chinese) samples with culturally specific pronatalist policy context, so generalization is uncertain; the proposed mediational pathway was not tested, as the authors acknowledge.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- Crisis does not reliably worsen mental health in the way the public narrative assumes. "Anxiety and depression fell among Ukrainian civilians even as the shelling got worse" (PMID 42831241) lands in the same place as last month's "The pandemic did not uniformly worsen existing mental illness — and bipolar disorder consistently improved" (PMID 42474420): when you actually measure the same people before and after, collective catastrophe produces flat or improving symptom trajectories at least as often as deterioration. Both also share the methodological moral — the alarming version of the story came from designs without a baseline.
- Sleep keeps surfacing as the hinge variable. Baseline sleep disturbance was the strongest predictor of who failed to improve in Ukraine (42831241); in the September batch, autonomic reactivity buffered loneliness specifically against depressive symptoms *and* sleep disturbance (PMID 42302916). Two very different designs pointing at sleep as the thing that blocks recovery rather than merely accompanying distress.

**Counterpoints**
- Last run's dominant thread was that self-report outperforms physiology as a marker of anxiety (42546511, 42632169, 42379500, 42302916). The Ukraine study is a useful corrective in the other direction: falling self-reported anxiety amid rising objective threat may partly be a shifting internal yardstick — recalibration, response shift, or attrition of the worst-affected — not improvement. Self-report is cheaper and sometimes better, but it is not a fixed ruler.
- Terror management theory's revival in "Reminding people of death makes them want children" (PMID 42833108) sits awkwardly beside the September batch's replication-minded entries — the partial failed replication in extinction research (42546511), the null primary comparison in the RECLAIM writing trial (PMID 42658633), and the overturning of frontal alpha as an anxiety marker (42379500). One batch is dismantling fragile paradigms; this new study leans on one of the most famously fragile.

**New themes**
- Anxiety as a response to macro-social conditions rather than to clinical or biological variables. All three new studies — war (42831241), post-consent-reform sexual norms (42844656), pronatalist policy and mortality salience (42833108) — locate the driver of anxiety in a societal shift. The September digest was almost entirely clinical and mechanistic (treatment formats, mediators, biomarkers); nothing there occupied this register except, loosely, the trans health-care disparity study (PMID 42658622).
- Qualitative and interview-based evidence enters the mix for the first time with the young men's sexual anxiety study (42844656); the previous digest contained no qualitative primary research at all.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** In all three studies, anxiety moves in the opposite direction to the objective conditions that are supposed to drive it. Ukrainian civilians got less anxious as artillery attacks and air raid alarms increased and hope for the counteroffensive collapsed (PMID 42831241); young men who came of age under a consent culture designed to make sex safer describe sex as a hazard to be defused rather than enjoyed (PMID 42844656); and reminding people of their own death — the ultimate threat — pushed them toward wanting children rather than away from risk, most strongly in those already chronically ill (PMID 42833108). Taken together, the batch suggests the fear thermostat is set by meaning, expectation and moral self-appraisal, not by a reading of actual danger.

**Why pitch this now:** Three separate policy areas — wartime and humanitarian mental health support, consent education, and pronatalist spending — are currently built on the assumption that changing the objective conditions will change how people feel, and these studies each suggest that assumption slips. It is also a rare chance to write about anxiety without a wearable, a scan or a drug in the frame.

**Angle:** A long-read on psychological recalibration — how quickly humans reset their fear baseline to whatever is now normal, who fails to reset (the ones not sleeping), and the uncomfortable corollary that falling anxiety scores can be a sign of adaptation rather than of wellbeing. Written for a general-interest reader living through their own slow adjustment to crisis news, with an honest spine about how thin and mismatched the underlying evidence still is.

Caveat for the commissioning conversation: this is a three-study pattern with 208 online respondents, 31 interviews, and a mortality-salience paradigm with a poor replication record behind it. It will only work as a feature if it is reported out with habituation, allostatic load and response-shift researchers rather than resting on these papers alone.

**Potential headlines:**
- What happens to fear when the danger stops going away
- The shelling got worse and the anxiety scores went down
- Your sense of threat stopped tracking the threat, and nobody tells you when it resets

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — fits the Mind desk's appetite for habituation and allostatic-load science, and the Ukraine prospective data gives it a hard news peg the desk can lead on.
- **The Atlantic** — ideas-driven readership already steeped in "the new normal" discourse; the piece supplies the empirical content that commentary on adaptation usually lacks.
- **Aeon** — the moral-self-appraisal strand from the young men's interviews and the death-anxiety-and-fertility material suit an essay about how people calibrate fear to meaning rather than probability.
- **BBC Future** — strong track record on the psychology of risk perception and habituation, and would handle the "lower scores are not the same as being well" nuance carefully.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Anxiety — October 2026
**Checked:** 2026-10-11 | **Studies reviewed:** 3
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

### Study 1: Anxiety and depression fell among Ukrainian civilians even as the shelling got worse
**PMID:** 42831241 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Causal language for an observational predictor** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "It also flags disrupted sleep as the thing that blocks that recalibration, which is a plausible, testable target for wartime mental health support."
- **Abstract says:** "Higher baseline sleep disturbance predicted smaller reductions in anxiety and depression… highlighting sleep as a potentially important target for mental health support under prolonged war-related stress."
- **Problem:** "The thing that blocks that recalibration" converts a prospective association into a mechanism. The study is observational with two waves; baseline sleep disturbance could be a marker of severity, comorbidity, or exposure rather than a blocking factor. The digest's own Caveats note the observational design, so the body text contradicts it here.
- **Suggested fix:** "It also identifies disrupted sleep as the baseline characteristic most consistently associated with smaller symptom reductions — which the authors suggest is a plausible, testable target for wartime mental health support."

**Issue B. "Strongest predictor" overstates the abstract's wording** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The strongest predictor of who failed to improve was baseline sleep disturbance"
- **Abstract says:** "Sleep disturbance emerged as a robust predictor of less favourable symptom change" / plain language summary: "the most consistent predictor of less favourable symptom change."
- **Problem:** "Most consistent" (i.e. predicted both anxiety and depression change) is not the same as "strongest" (largest effect size). No effect sizes are given in the abstract.
- **Suggested fix:** "The most consistent predictor of who failed to improve was baseline sleep disturbance"

**Issue C. Internal inconsistency on the interval** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "scoring lower on anxiety than they did five months earlier"
- **Abstract says:** "a pivotal six-month period in 2023"; waves in June 2023 and November 2023.
- **Problem:** The body text correctly says "those six months"; the pitch angle says "five months earlier." Pick the abstract's framing to avoid an inconsistency a sub-editor will query.
- **Suggested fix:** "scoring lower on anxiety than they did six months earlier"

**Issue D. NS fit score of 7 on a small self-report sample** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 — a genuinely surprising prospective result from an under-studied natural experiment, held back by a small, skewed online sample."
- **Abstract says:** "two-wave online longitudinal study of 208 Ukrainian civilian adults (80.8% female; mean age 29.4 years)"; all outcomes self-reported; no control condition.
- **Problem:** A 208-person, 81%-female online convenience sample with two self-report waves and no pre-war baseline is thin for a 7. The counterintuitive angle is strong, but the evidence base is not. The score note already concedes the weakness, which argues for lowering the number rather than annotating it.
- **Suggested fix:** "**NS fit:** 6/10 — a genuinely surprising prospective result from an under-studied natural experiment, but a small, skewed, self-report online sample limits how hard the finding can be pushed."

---

### Study 2: Young men describe sex as a hazard to defuse rather than something to enjoy
**PMID:** 42844656 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Shifts from… to" misstates an additive finding** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the operative question shifts from 'does she want this?' to 'am I the kind of man who could get this wrong?'"
- **Abstract says:** "the question when navigating consent is often not only 'does she want this?' but 'am I the kind of man who could get this wrong?'"
- **Problem:** The abstract describes a second question layered on top of the first, not a replacement of it. The digest's version implies the men stopped attending to the partner's wishes, which is a materially different and more provocative claim.
- **Suggested fix:** "the operative question is often not only 'does she want this?' but also 'am I the kind of man who could get this wrong?'"

**Issue B. Quantifying a qualitative finding** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "shame that came as much from self-criticism as from anyone else's accusation" and "the harshest accuser in the room is usually the man himself"
- **Abstract says:** "shame arose not only from accusations by others, but also from self-criticism."
- **Problem:** "As much as" and "usually" assign relative weight and frequency that 31 thematically analyzed interviews cannot support, and the digest's own Caveats state that "no prevalence claim is possible." The body and pitch text contradict that caveat.
- **Suggested fix:** Body: "and shame that arose not only from others' accusations but also from self-criticism." Pitch: "and that for some of these men the accuser they described most vividly was themselves."

**Issue C. Causal framing of participants' own attribution** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "a cultural shift intended to make sex safer has, for some men, produced a vigilance state that crowds out pleasure entirely"
- **Abstract says:** "They attributed this wariness to the cultural climate that surrounds consent" and "a cultural suspicion of men appears to have been internalized by some young men."
- **Problem:** The causal link is the participants' own interpretation, reported in interviews — not something the design can measure. The digest's Caveats say exactly this, so the pitch angle contradicts its own caveat. "Crowds out pleasure entirely" also hardens "how rarely these men described enjoying sex" into an absolute.
- **Suggested fix:** "these men themselves link their wariness to the cultural climate around consent — and describe a vigilance state in which they rarely mentioned enjoying sex at all"

**Issue D. Author first name not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Call Jess Forrest at the Melbourne School of Public Health"
- **Abstract says:** "Forrest J(1)… (1)Melbourne School of Public Health, University of Melbourne, Melbourne, Australia."
- **Problem:** The affiliation is correct, but the given name "Jess" is unverifiable from abstract only. Confirm before the pitch goes out.
- **Suggested fix:** "Call lead author J. Forrest at the Melbourne School of Public Health, University of Melbourne [confirm first name]"

---

### Study 3: Reminding people of death makes them want children — and the effect is strongest in the chronically ill
**PMID:** 42833108 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

The headline's causal phrasing is defensible here — these are randomized priming experiments, not observational data — and "want children" correctly tracks the measured outcome (intentions), which the Caveats reinforce. The treatment of the untested mediational chain, the replication problem with mortality-salience work, and the unreported sample sizes is accurate and appropriately hedged.

**Issue A. Participant nationality not stated in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Across three experiments with Chinese adults — including a sample of people with chronic illnesses"
- **Abstract says:** "Participants included general adults and individuals with chronic illnesses." Author affiliations are Shandong Normal University and Henan University of Engineering, China.
- **Problem:** Chinese samples are a reasonable inference from the affiliations and the paper's pronatalist-policy framing, but the abstract never states participant nationality. Unverifiable from abstract only — and the Caveats lean on it ("single-country (Chinese) samples").
- **Suggested fix:** "Across three experiments run by a Chinese research group — including a sample of people with chronic illnesses" [confirm participant nationality from full text]
